question: An organization has \(30\) employees, \(20\) of whom have a brand A computer while the other \(10\) have a brand B computer. For security, the computers can only be connected to each other and only by cables. The cables can only connect a brand A computer to a brand B computer. Employees can communicate with each other if their computers are directly connected by a cable or by relaying messages through a series of connected computers. Initially, no computer is connected to any other. A technician arbitrarily selects one computer of each brand and installs a cable between them, provided there is not already a cable between that pair. The technician stops once every employee can communicate with each other. What is the maximum possible number of cables used?
solution:
A brand B computer connected to all 20 brand A computers would put all the brand A computers in one communicating group. We can force such a computer by counting cables.

Suppose 191 cables have been installed. If every brand B computer had at most 19 cables, there would be at most
\[
10\cdot19=190
\]
cables altogether, since each cable touches exactly one brand B computer. Therefore some brand B computer, call it \(B_*\), connects directly to all 20 brand A computers.

Every other brand B computer must have at least one cable: if one had none, only \(20\cdot9=180\) cables could exist. Each brand B computer can consequently reach \(B_*\) through a brand A computer. Thus the entire network is connected whenever 191 cables are present, so the technician must stop by then.

To attain this bound, leave one brand A computer isolated and install every cable between the remaining 19 brand A computers and all 10 brand B computers. This uses
\[
19\cdot10=190
\]
cables, and the isolated computer prevents the technician from stopping at any earlier stage. The other 29 computers now communicate with one another. One final cable from the isolated computer to any brand B computer connects everyone.

The maximum is therefore \(190+1=\boxed{191}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Immediately before the final cable is installed, the network is disconnected. Counting the connections missing between separate groups will bound how many cables can already be present.

There are \(20\cdot10=200\) possible cables. Choose one communicating group, meaning all computers reachable from a chosen computer. Let it contain \(a\) brand A computers and \(b\) brand B computers. The group is nonempty and does not contain everyone.

No cable joins this group to the remaining computers. The number of such absent possible cables is
\[
a(10-b)+(20-a)b.
\]
The first term counts brand A computers inside paired with brand B computers outside; the second counts the reverse arrangement. These are distinct pairs.

This number is always at least 10:

- If \(a=0\), then \(b\ge1\), so there are \(20b\ge20\) absent cables.
- If \(a=20\), then \(b\le9\), so there are \(20(10-b)\ge20\) absent cables.
- If \(1\le a\le19\), both \(a\) and \(20-a\) are at least 1. Therefore
\[
a(10-b)+(20-a)b\ge(10-b)+b=10.
\]
Thus any disconnected network has at most \(200-10=190\) cables. Adding its final cable gives at most 191.

This is attainable: keep one brand A computer isolated while installing all \(19\cdot10=190\) cables among the other 29 computers, then connect the isolated computer to a brand B computer. The maximum is \(\boxed{191}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count missing connections
